newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: ACCESS PREDICTS ECONOMY TO IMPROVE LATE '97
Finance analysts Access Economics predict Australia's economy will stay weak before picking up in 12 months.
Access Economics today released its September quarter, five-year business outlook.
It expects unemployment will worsen up until mid 1997, but improve near the end of that year.
One of the Directors, Chris Richardson, says for much of Australia, the next 12 months will be fairly weak economically, with bright spots in communications and mining.
But, he expects the economy will pick-up in late 1997, due to better growth in both Japan and the United States, and because housing will finally turn around.
The Access Economics outlook also suggests a cut in interest rates should be off the agenda until late 1997.
CALL FOR HERRON TO BE CALLED TO ACCOUNT
A Northern Territory politician says Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron has shown gross insensitivity to Aborigines, and a lack of appreciation of the richness of indigenous culture.
MLA Neil Bell says the Minister showed this most recently with a claim an un-named female Aboriginal leader would have wound up married to a remote elder if she hadn't been taken from her family.
Mr Bell says the comment maligns Aboriginal elders, and casts doubt on whether Senator Herron is up to the job.
He says it's time Senator Herron was called to account for his handling of the portfolio.
WAR OF WORDS OVER INQUIRY COMMENTS

Northern Territory chief minister, Shane Stone, has accused Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Social Justice Commissioner, Mick Dodson, of encouraging indigenous people to fear the Federal Government.

The accusation follows Mr Dodson's response to a letter written by Prime Minister John Howard, which questioned the usefulness of the inquiry into the forced separation of Aboriginal children from their families.
Mr Dodson says Mr Howard's attitude is callous.
But Mr Stone says Mr Dodson is guilty of using double standards, because he is happy to criticise the Prime Minister, while dismissing any criticism of himself as racist.
FAIRA CALLS ON QLD GOVT TO ACCEPT FINDINGS

The Foundation for Aboriginal and Islander Research Action says the Queensland Government has the chance to further reconciliation by accepting fully a decision by the Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission.
Last week, the Commission upheld complaints by six Palm Island workers who claimed the Government discriminated against them by paying them wages at a rate less than non-aboriginal workers.
FAIRA spokesman Les Maelzer says despite the breaches of the Racial Discrimination Act being up to 21 years old, the decision recognises one of the many wrongs of the past.
Mr Maelzer says he understands one of cabinet's considerations will be the cost of the recommendations for compensation, but he says justice, not economic pragmatism, should be the criteria.
PILOTS LACK CERTAIN SKILLS - INQUIRY TOLD
A military inquiry into the Blackhawk air disaster has heard that pilots don't have the required level of skill to cope with a real life counter terrorist operation.
Pilot, Lieutenant Richard Garvey, told the inquiry yesterday that they'd need several weeks to prepare for a terrorist situation.
He said the proficiency of the 5th Aviation Regiment had improved in the past year, but training would be needed to bring it up to the required standard to handle a terrorist attack.
In Perth this morning, Lieutenant Garvey will continue giving evidence to the inquiry into the crash of two Blackhawk helicopters during an exercise near Townsville in June.
AMA WARNS AGAINST EXPERIMENTING
The Australian Medical Association is warning people against experimenting with drugs they know little or nothing about.
Four people are still in hospital in a stable condition, after consuming the designer drug Fantasy at a Broadbeach dance club at the weekend.
AMA Queensland Branch spokesman, Doctor Bob Brown, says the drug's danger lies in the severe effects that can be caused with small doses.
Doctor Brown says the effects are also magnified when the drug is mixed with other drugs, including alcohol.
He says he's particularly concerned about the dangers with schoolies week coming up.
HORAN WANTS FANTASY BANNED
Queensland's Health Minister, Mike Horan, says he wants the drug Fantasy made illegal immediately.
The drug -- known as GHB or gamma hydroxy-butyric -- put ten people in hospital on the Gold Coast at the weekend after they consumed it at a Broadbeach Dance club.
Mr Horan will hold urgent talks on the incident, with his federal and state counterparts .
Speaking at the launch of a drug information guide for parents, Mr Horan said he would also consult with his Cabinet colleagues regarding the regulation of dance parties.
CJC INQUIRY MAY START NEXT WEEK
In Queensland, the judicial inquiry into the role of the Criminal Justice Commission could be underway as early as next week.
The inquiry will examine the CJC's finances and whether any of its operations can be carried out by other agencies.
It will be headed by retired Supreme Court judges Peter Connolly and Kevin Ryan.
The state's Attorney General, Denver Beanland, denies that the inquiry will be a politically motivated witch-hunt.
Mr Beanland says the effectiveness of the Parliamentary Criminal Justice Committee in dealing with the CJC will also be examined.
The Opposition says the inquiry aims to minimise the damage to the government from a CJC inspired inquiry into a pre-election deal between the Coalition and the Police Union.
